implementation_notes: Swift standardizes on initializers, so the alternative construction routes are convenience initializers that delegate to the designated one, and failure is expressed inside the initializer as init? rather than through a separate factory (the standard library does this with Int(exactly:), UIImage(named:) and Array(repeating:count:)). Keep stored properties let and validate before assigning so a failed initializer returns nil instead of a partially built value; the classic static-factory structure is only needed where an initializer cannot express the operation (see the sibling variant).
pitfalls: A failable initializer must return nil before assigning stored properties in a class hierarchy, or a partially initialized object can escape through a throwing/delegating path - validate first, assign last.

Convenience initializers cannot reach a superclass initializer directly; they must delegate sideways to a designated initializer of the same class, and `required` initializers have to be re-declared by subclasses.

Adding an initializer to a struct body suppresses the synthesized memberwise initializer, silently breaking callers that used it - put the alternative route in an extension or use the factory-function variant.

variants.name: Static factory functions (make/from)
variants.implementation_notes: Use a static factory function when the creation route must return a sibling, protocol or generic-specialized type (static func make() -> any Shape), when a generic initializer cannot express the constraints, or when adding an initializer would suppress the synthesized memberwise initializer. The function can return an optional or throw instead of being failable, and it is the only route that keeps the concrete type hidden behind a protocol; it cannot, however, be dynamically dispatched the way initializers are.
pitfalls: A static factory cannot be specialized by subclasses the way a `required` initializer can; if creation must vary per subclass, an initializer is the right mechanism.
Factories that only forward arguments duplicate the memberwise initializer and hide the type's canonical creation route - keep the factory set small and document it.
Returning an existential (any Shape) erases the concrete type for callers; return the concrete type unless hiding the implementation is the actual goal.
